introduction.p: The following notes are intended to remind you what we covered each week. They are not a substitute for attending class and not a substitute for reading the textbook.
The first two weeks of class focus on some prerequisite understanding necessary for our later conversations about functions and their analysis.

subsection.title: P1 Linear Modeling
subsection.p: I can calculate a slope as a rate of change and use it with the point-slope equation of a line to model a linear relation between two variables.

What do I need to understand?
Conceptual: A slope is a proportionality constant relating the change in a dependent variable with respect to the change in an independent variable, usually written \Delta y = m \cdot \Delta x, where m represents the slope, \Delta x represents the increment of change in the independent variable x, and \Delta y represents the increment of change in the dependent variable y.
The variables x and y represent abstract placeholders for more physically relevant variables. you will need to be able to use other variables.
Computational: Calculate the slope between two points, (x_1,y_1) and (x_2,y_2) as
m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.
Modeling: Although you likely currently feel most comfortable with the slope-intercept equation of a line y=mx+b, I am asking you to begin thinking in terms of the point-slope equation of a line given by y = y_1 + m \cdot(x-x_1) where m represents the known slope and (x_1,y_1) represents a known point on the line.
This model of a line physically thinks through the process as follows. We know when x=x_1, the value of y starts at y=y_1 (because it is on the line). As x changes to any other value, the value of y also changes, and the slope gives the proportional amount of change:
y \amp = y_1 + \Delta y \amp = y_1 + m \cdot \Delta x \amp = y_1 + m \cdot (x-x_1)
It is this idea that generalizes later in calculus to the idea of a definite integral measuring the change \Delta y when the rate of change or slope f'(t) is not constant:
y = y_1 + \int_{x_1}^{x} f'(t) \, dt . You are not expected to understand this bit yet -- it is a preview to the future.

statement.p: When a company sets the price of its product at $, it is able to sell items per day. When it changes the price to $, it is able to sell items per day. Create a linear model using the point-slope equation for the number of items sold per day S as a function of the company's price p.

subsection.title: P2 Intervals and Set Operations
subsection.p: I can translate a graphical representation of a set of numbers back and forth to interval notation and compute unions and intersections of multiple such sets.

What do I need to understand?
A collection of real numbers is a set. Simple sets with a finite number of values can be expressed using curly braces listing the numbers separated by commas, such as \{-3,2,5/}, which is a set including the values of -3, 2, and 5.
We often deal with sets formed by intervals, which are sets that include all of the values between two endpoints, and possibly the endpoints as well.
A single interval (a,b), where a and b represent any real numbers with a \lt b (or possibly -\infty or \infty), describes the set of values between a and b. It corresponds to the set of values x such that a \lt x \lt b, which in set constructor notation is
(a,b) = \{x : a \lt x \lt b\} . This type of interval where the endpoints are not included is called an open interval.
In order to describe an interval where the endpoint is included, we change the round parenthesis into a square bracket on the endpoint that is included.
[a,b) = \{x : a \le x \lt b\} (a,b] = \{x : a \lt x \le b\} [a,b] = \{x : a \le x \le b\}
When both endpoints are included, the interval is called a closed interval.
The graphical representation of an interval is created by drawing a line segment between the endpoints, and marking the endpoints themselves with either open circles (if not included) or closed circles (if included). If the interval extends to infinity, instead of putting a circle on that end, we put an arrow to indicate it continues indefinitely.
When a set includes values coming from multiple disconnected or disjoint intervals, we describe the set as a union of the component intervals. A single isolated number a can also be included as a set \{a\}.
Suppose my set S has component intervals or isolated values that can be described individually as S_1, S_2, S_3, etc. Then we would write
S = S_1 \cup S_2 \cup S_3 \cup \cdots
Using the union operation \cup creates a single set from many component pieces.
Given two sets A and B, the union is a new set A \cup B that consists of all values in at least one of the two sets (could be in just one or both).
Given two sets A and B, the intersection is a new set A \cap B that consists of all values in both the two sets (must be in both). This is the values in the overlap
After you identify the values in a set, you then identify the new component intervals and possible isolated values to rewrite the set using interval notation.

introduction.p: These are copies of the in-class activities distributed during the semester.

li.p: Recognize a proportional relationship between two variables and identify its proportionality constant.
Calculate slope as an average rate of change, and explain why it does not depend on which two data points are used to compute it.
Write the equation of a linear relation in point-slope form, understood as a starting value plus an amount of change.

introduction.p: Today's activity is our first as a class using this format. You will work in your assigned group, moving through the questions together rather than racing ahead individually — the goal is that everyone in the group can explain why an answer is correct, not just what the answer is.
Each group member takes one of the following roles for the activity:

row.cell: Keeps the group on task and on pace; makes sure everyone has spoken before the group moves on; asks the instructor for help if the group is stuck after trying on its own.
Writes the group's agreed-on answers, in the group's own words; notes any question the group could not resolve.
Speaks for the group during whole-class discussion and can explain why the group answered as it did, not just what was written.
Checks in periodically on whether everyone understands, not just whether the group is moving forward; leads a short end-of-activity check-in on what worked.

introduction.p: In a group of three, the Manager also takes on the Reflector's check-in duties.
Gasoline at a particular station costs \$3.25 per gallon. The table below shows the price paid for several purchase amounts. Fill in the two missing entries before answering the questions.

statement.p: For each column, compute (price paid) ÷ (gallons purchased). What do you notice?
Pick two different columns and compute (change in price) ÷ (change in gallons) between them. Then try a different pair of columns. Does the pair you choose matter? Explain.
Write a sentence describing price in terms of gallons purchased, using the constant you found (for example, “price is ___ times the number of gallons”).
If a customer purchased 0 gallons, what would they pay? Why must this be true for this kind of relationship between two variables?

introduction.p: A veterinarian prescribes a medication at a fixed rate of 5 mg per kilogram of the animal's body weight.

statement.p: Fill in the missing dose. What is the proportionality constant here, and what does it mean physically?
Without adding a new column to the table, predict the dose for a 25 kg animal.

exercise.title: Model 2: Mile Markers on the Highway

introduction.p: A car is driving on a highway at a constant speed. A passenger records the mile marker the car is passing at several clock times.

statement.p: Between 1:15 pm and 1:45 pm, how much time passed, and how many miles did the marker increase? Express this as a rate (miles per minute, or miles per hour).
Compute the same kind of rate using the 2:15 pm and 2:45 pm readings, and again using the 1:15 pm and 2:15 pm readings. What do you notice? What everyday word describes this rate?

Does doubling the elapsed time double the mile marker? Check using the numbers in the table. Is the mile marker proportional to the clock time? Compare this to what you found about the price of gas in Model 1, and explain the difference.

Using the 1:15 pm reading and the rate you found, write an equation for the mile marker M in terms of t, the number of hours after 1:15 pm. Write your equation as (starting mile marker) plus (rate times hours elapsed).
Use your equation to predict the mile marker at 12:45 pm, before the table begins. Was this point one you already had recorded?

The constant rate you found in Model 2 is called the slope of the relation, or its average rate of change. The equation you built in Task 4 has the same structure as y - y_1 = m(x - x_1), called point-slope form, where (x_1, y_1) is any known point on the relation and m is the slope. It says exactly what you wrote: a new value equals a starting value plus the slope times how far you've moved from that starting point.

exercise.title: Applying the Idea: A Growing Plant

introduction.p: A plant is measured twice after it is potted: it is 4 inches tall after 2 weeks, and 10 inches tall after 5 weeks. Assume it grows at a constant rate.

statement.p: Find the plant's growth rate, in inches per week.
Using one of the two given measurements, write an equation for the plant's height h in terms of the number of weeks w since it was potted, in point-slope form.

Use your equation to find the plant's height when w = 0. Does it make sense for a newly potted plant to already have some height? Was the plant's height proportional to the number of weeks since potting? Explain.
Rewrite your equation in the form h = mw + b. What does b represent in this situation? Was it one of the two measurements you were originally given?
Predict the plant's height at w = 8 weeks.
